message.content: {"passages":[{"reference":"1.5","text":"What, then, must be done except this? I will travel to Egypt, become friends with the hierophants and prophets of the inner sanctuaries, and, after searching for and finding a magician, persuade him with a great deal of money to perform a raising up of a soul (what is called necromancy), while I inquire as though about some particular matter. But the inquiry will be about learning whether the soul is immortal. And I will know the soul’s answer—that it is immortal—not from its speaking or even from hearing it, but merely from its being seen, so that, after seeing it with my own eyes, I may have a self-sufficient and adequate conclusion, from the mere fact that it appeared, that it exists. Then the obscure words belonging to hearing will no longer be able to overturn the eyes’ own evidence. Nevertheless, I put this very consideration before a philosopher of my acquaintance, who advised me on many grounds not to dare such a thing. “For if the soul does not heed the magician,” he said, “you will live with a guilty conscience because you acted against the laws that forbid people to do these things. But if it does heed him, then, besides your living with a guilty conscience, I think that the concerns of piety will no longer prosper for you—the very thing for whose sake you dared it. For they say that the divine is hostile toward those who harass souls at the dissolution of dead bodies.” When I heard this, I became more hesitant about attempting such a thing, but I did not abandon the plan I had formed from the beginning. Rather, as one whose impulse had been obstructed, I was disheartened.","lexical_decisions":[{"source_quote":"ψυχῆς ἀναπομπὴν (τὴν λεγομένην νεκρομαντείαν)","chosen":"a raising up of a soul (what is called necromancy)","rationale":"ἀναπομπή conveys an upward sending or raising, while the parenthesis explicitly names the practice."},{"source_quote":"οὐκ ἐκ τοῦ λαλῆσαι ἢ καὶ ἀκοῦσαι ἔσται μοι γνῶναι","chosen":"I will know ... not from its speaking or even from hearing it","rationale":"Preserves the distinction between verbal or auditory evidence and the visual evidence that follows."},{"source_quote":"τὰ τῶν ὀφθαλμῶν ἴδια τὰ τῆς ἀκοῆς ἀνατρέψαι ἄδηλα ῥήματα","chosen":"the obscure words belonging to hearing ... overturn the eyes’ own evidence","rationale":"Keeps the contrast between what is peculiar to sight and the unclear words received through hearing."},{"source_quote":"κατὰ πολλοὺς τρόπους","chosen":"on many grounds","rationale":"The phrase indicates that the philosopher offered multiple considerations against the plan."},{"source_quote":"ἐπὶ τοῖς τῇ λύσει θανόντων σωμάτων σκύλλουσιν τὰς ψυχάς","chosen":"toward those who harass souls at the dissolution of dead bodies","rationale":"σκύλλω conveys troubling or harassing, while λύσις retains the image of bodily dissolution."}],"source_issues":[]},{"reference":"1.6","text":"And, so that I may not recount such things to you at great length, while I was amid so many thoughts and affairs, a report arose quietly during the reign of Tiberius Caesar. Taking its beginning from the spring equinox, it continually grew and, like a truly good messenger of God, traveled throughout the world, unable to conceal God’s will in silence. Continually, therefore, it became more widespread and greater, saying that once a certain man in Judea, having begun at the spring equinox, was proclaiming to the Jews the kingdom of the eternal God, which he said any one of them would enjoy if he first set his way of life right. And in order that he might be believed to do these things because he was full of divinity, he performed many marvelous signs and wonders by command alone, as one who had received the authority from God. For he makes the deaf hear and the blind regain their sight; he makes those with deformed limbs walk and sets the lame upright; he drives away every disease and puts every demon to flight. Even lepers and people with scabies go away healed merely by gazing intently at him from a distance. Dead people who are brought to him are raised, and there is nothing that he is unable to do. Indeed, the farther time advanced, the truth of the matter became much greater and more firmly established through an increasing number of visitors—no longer the report, I mean. For by then gatherings were even being held in various places for deliberation and inquiry into who the one who had appeared might be and what he meant by what he said.","lexical_decisions":[{"source_quote":"ἐξ ἐαρινῆς τροπῆς","chosen":"from the spring equinox","rationale":"The seasonal τροπή is understood as the spring turning point, conventionally the equinox."},{"source_quote":"ὡς ἀληθῶς ἀγαθὴ θεοῦ ἄγγελος","chosen":"like a truly good messenger of God","rationale":"The report is personified as a messenger traveling through the world."},{"source_quote":"τὸ τοῦ θεοῦ βούλημα σιγᾶν στέγειν μὴ δυναμένη","chosen":"unable to conceal God’s will in silence","rationale":"στέγω is taken as concealing or keeping covered, with silence as the means."},{"source_quote":"προκατορθώσῃ τὴν πολιτείαν","chosen":"first set his way of life right","rationale":"The verb conveys prior rectification, while πολιτεία here denotes conduct or manner of life."},{"source_quote":"κυλλοὺς ποιεῖ περιπατεῖν, χωλοὺς ἀνορθοῖ","chosen":"he makes those with deformed limbs walk and sets the lame upright","rationale":"Uses distinct descriptions for κυλλοί and χωλοί rather than merging the two clauses."},{"source_quote":"λεπροὶ ψωροὶ ἐκ διαστήματος μόνον ἐνορῶντες αὐτῷ","chosen":"lepers and people with scabies ... merely by gazing intently at him from a distance","rationale":"Preserves both skin-condition terms and the stated distance from which they look at him."},{"source_quote":"οὐκέτι φήμη λέγω, ἀλλὰ τοῦ πράγματος ἡ ἀλήθεια","chosen":"the truth of the matter ... no longer the report, I mean","rationale":"Preserves the narrator’s explicit correction from speaking of a report to speaking of the reality itself."}],"source_issues":[{"source_quote":"τὴν. τοῦ ἀιδίου θεοῦ","issue":"The supplied reading places a full stop between the article and its dependent genitive phrase. The translation construes the words continuously as an editorial punctuation feature; this is not treated as an OCR error.","proposed_reading":"τὴν τοῦ ἀιδίου θεοῦ","blocks_publication":false}]},{"reference":"1.7","text":"Then, once in that same year, at the autumn equinox, someone stood publicly and cried out, saying, “Men of Rome, listen! The Son of God is present in Judea, promising eternal life to all who desire it, if they live in accordance with the will of the Father who sent him. Therefore change your way of life from worse things to better, from temporary things to eternal. Know that there is one God, the heavenly one, whose world you inhabit unjustly before his righteous eyes. But if you change and live according to his will, then, after being carried into another age and becoming everlasting, you will enjoy his inexpressible good things. If, however, you disobey, your souls, after the dissolution of the body, will be cast into the place of fire, where, being punished everlastingly, they will reorient themselves to no avail. For each person’s present life is the time for reorientation.” When I heard these things, I was distressed that no one from among so many crowds, after hearing so momentous an announcement, had said, “I will travel to Judea so that I may see whether this man is speaking the truth when he says these things,” considering that the Son of God had come to Judea, revealing the will of the Father who sent him for the sake of a good and eternal hope, especially since what they say he proclaims is no small matter. For he firmly declares that the souls of some, being eternal, will enjoy eternal good things, whereas the souls of others, after being cast into unquenchable fire, will be punished throughout the age.","lexical_decisions":[{"source_quote":"πρὸς αὐτῷ τῷ ἔτει","chosen":"in that same year","rationale":"The phrase locates the public proclamation within the year already under discussion."},{"source_quote":"Ἄνδρες Ῥωμαῖοι","chosen":"Men of Rome","rationale":"Preserves both the direct address to men and their identification as Romans."},{"source_quote":"μεταβάλλεσθε τὸν τρόπον","chosen":"change your way of life","rationale":"The verb is μεταβάλλω, and its object identifies the manner or course of life to be changed."},{"source_quote":"ἀνωφέλητα μετανοήσουσιν","chosen":"they will reorient themselves to no avail","rationale":"Uses the supplied terminology for μετανοέω while retaining the explicit claim that this response will be ineffective."},{"source_quote":"ὁ γὰρ τῆς μετανοίας καιρὸς ἡ νῦν ἑκάστου ζωὴ τυγχάνει","chosen":"For each person’s present life is the time for reorientation","rationale":"Uses the corresponding terminology for μετάνοια without adding a destination absent from the source."},{"source_quote":"ὧν μὲν γὰρ τὰς ψυχὰς διαβεβαιοῦται αἰωνίους οὔσας αἰωνίων ἀπολαύσειν ἀγαθῶν, ὧν δὲ ἐν πυρὶ ἀσβέστῳ ῥιφείσας τὸν αἰῶνα κολασθήσεσθαι","chosen":"the souls of some, being eternal, will enjoy eternal good things, whereas the souls of others ... will be punished throughout the age","rationale":"Preserves the contrast between the two groups of souls and renders τὸν αἰῶνα as an expression of duration."}],"source_issues":[{"source_quote":"σώματος·λύσιν","issue":"The supplied reading places a medial stop between the dependent genitive and λύσιν. The translation construes the phrase continuously as an editorial punctuation feature; this is not treated as an OCR error.","proposed_reading":"σώματος λύσιν","blocks_publication":false},{"source_quote":"ὡς ὅτι υἱὸς θεοῦ ἐπιδεδήμηκεν τῇ Ἰουδαίᾳ","issue":"The precise discourse force of ὡς ὅτι is uncertain. The translation takes the sequence as introducing the consideration that makes the crowds’ inaction distressing, but an explanatory rendering such as “seeing that” is also possible without changing the supplied text.","proposed_reading":"","blocks_publication":true}]},{"reference":"1.8","text":"While saying these things about others, I also addressed myself, saying, “Why do I blame others when I am under the same charge of negligence? Rather, I will set out for Judea, after first putting my life in order.” Yet, after I had resolved on this course, a long period of delay followed, because the affairs of life were difficult to break free from. At last, then, having somehow reflected in this way on the nature of life—that by entangling those who are eager to act in hope, it lies in wait for them—and also on the time for which I had somehow been drawn in unawares, tossed about by hopes, and on the fact that, while occupied in this way, we human beings die, I left everything of mine just as it happened to be and set out for Portus. After reaching the harbor and putting out to sea, I was carried by the hostility of the winds to Alexandria instead of Judea. Then, detained there by a lack of winds, I associated with the philosophers and related the accounts concerning the report and the man who had appeared in Rome. But they answered, “We do not know the man who appeared in Rome. Concerning the one who had arisen in Judea and was called the Son of God by the report, however, we too have heard from many who had come from there, and we have learned about all the wonders he performed while speaking.”","lexical_decisions":[{"source_quote":"πρότερον τὸν ἐμὸν διαθεὶς βίον","chosen":"after first putting my life in order","rationale":"διατίθημι here indicates arranging or settling one’s life and affairs before departure."},{"source_quote":"τῶν βιωτικῶν πραγμάτων δυσεκλύτων ὄντων","chosen":"because the affairs of life were difficult to break free from","rationale":"Preserves both the practical affairs denoted by βιωτικά and the difficulty of disengagement."},{"source_quote":"ἐλπίδι ἐμπλέκων τοὺς σπεύδοντας ἐνεδρεύει","chosen":"by entangling those who are eager to act in hope, it lies in wait for them","rationale":"Retains the paired images of entanglement and ambush used to characterize life."},{"source_quote":"τὰ πάντα μου ὡς ἔτυχεν ἀφεὶς","chosen":"I left everything of mine just as it happened to be","rationale":"Indicates that he departed without first arranging everything he possessed."},{"source_quote":"ἀνέμων ἔχθραις","chosen":"by the hostility of the winds","rationale":"Retains the source’s personification of the adverse winds."},{"source_quote":"ἀνέμων ἀπορίᾳ","chosen":"by a lack of winds","rationale":"Here ἀπορία denotes the absence or insufficiency of wind needed for onward sailing."},{"source_quote":"περὶ πάντων ὧν λαλῶν ἐποίει θαυμασίων","chosen":"about all the wonders he performed while speaking","rationale":"The participle is rendered as contemporaneous, though an instrumental sense, “by speaking,” remains possible."}],"source_issues":[{"source_quote":"οὐ μὴν ἀλλὰ καὶ. ὃν ποτε","issue":"The supplied full stop interrupts the correlative expression and separates it from the additional object of reflection. The translation construes the expression continuously as an editorial punctuation feature; this is not treated as an OCR error.","proposed_reading":"οὐ μὴν ἀλλὰ καὶ ὃν ποτε","blocks_publication":false},{"source_quote":"ὃν ποτε εἰσεκλάπην χρόνον ἐλπίσιν δονούμενος","issue":"The construction is semantically difficult, especially the force of εἰσεκλάπην with the accusative χρόνον. The translation understands Clement as having been drawn in unawares for a period while being tossed about by hopes, but the exact sense remains unresolved.","proposed_reading":"","blocks_publication":true}]}]}
